one_liner: Go client/server framework sending typed Command objects over raw TCP/TLS; author benchmark shows 3.1-4.6x grpc-go echo QPS.
what_it_does: Replaces request/response RPC with a Distributed Command Pattern. A Command is a Go struct with Exec(ctx, receiver, proxy); the client serializes it onto a long-lived TCP/TLS connection, and the server decodes it and runs Exec against your Receiver, which sends one or more Results back through the Proxy, so server streaming is built in. The high-level Sender.Send(ctx, cmd) returns a core.Result that you type-assert, and a Group round-robins over N pre-dialed connections to one address. It is not wire- or API-compatible with gRPC: there are no .proto services and no HTTP/2, both ends must be Go, and every Command and Result type has to be registered with a codec (JSON, Protobuf or generated MUS).
how_it_is_fast: Each message on the connection is a varint sequence number, a type tag and the payload, with no HTTP/2 frames, HPACK headers or per-stream flow control, and many concurrent Commands share one connection. Writes go into a bufio.Writer, and a CAS flag coalesces flushes on both client and server, so concurrent senders on a connection share one Flush (one write syscall). The MUS codec (mus-stream-go) writes generated serializers straight into the stream, while the JSON and Protobuf codecs marshal into a temporary []byte first. The transport, not the codec, gives most of the gain: cmd-stream with the Protobuf codec still reaches 2.4-3.5x grpc-go QPS, and in the fixed run MUS used about 16 allocs and 3 KB per request against about 139 allocs and 12 KB for grpc-go.
when_to_use: Go-only service-to-service links where you own both client and server and need neither gRPC interop nor gRPC tooling.

Throughput-bound fan-in with a very large number of small requests in flight at once (the benchmark used 17-1024 B payloads, all fired at once), where grpc-go's per-call CPU and allocation cost is the bottleneck.
Workloads that already fit a command/job model (sagas, persisted or replayable commands), or that need several Results per request without HTTP/2 streaming.
Teams that can add generated MUS serializers for peak speed. If you keep .proto messages, the Protobuf codec still measured 2.4-3.5x grpc-go in the author's run.
when_not_to_use: Polyglot systems or public APIs. It is Go-only with a custom wire format: no gRPC or HTTP interop, and no grpcurl, gRPC-Gateway or service-mesh support.
Latency-bound calls across a real network. The only published numbers are from localhost on one laptop, and the author agreed on HN that they measure protocol overhead, not network latency.

When you need built-in compression, application-level retries, server-side cancellation/deadline propagation, or multi-endpoint balancing. The author says on HN that compression and retries are not provided, and the other two are missing from the code: Sender dials a single address and ctx only bounds the client-side wait.

Servers exposed to untrusted clients without extra hardening. Every Command runs in its own goroutine with no per-connection concurrency limit, the JSON and Protobuf codecs accept any payload length unless WithMaxLen is set, and authentication is mTLS only.

Risk-averse production use. The API is pre-1.0 (v0.7.3) and v0.7.0 (May 2026) changed the Cmd.Exec signature. One maintainer wrote 234 of 236 commits, and pkg.go.dev lists no importers outside the author's own repos.

integration.dependencies: mus-format/mus-stream-go, mus-format/common-go, ymz-ncnk/jointwork-go, plus one codec module (codec-json-go, codec-protobuf-go or codec-mus-stream-go; the Protobuf and MUS codecs need code generation)
integration.platforms: Any Go target. Built on net.Conn: TCP, TLS and mutual TLS are documented, and NewClient accepts any net.Conn
integration.thread_safety: Client and Sender are documented as thread-safe and multiplex concurrent Sends. The server runs each Command in its own goroutine, so the Receiver/Invoker must be thread-safe (documented), and Proxy.Send must be safe to call from several goroutines

gotchas: Server WorkersCount (default 8) is the maximum number of connections served at once. Each worker owns one connection for that connection's whole life, and later connections wait in a queue. Size it to your total client connections, as the benchmark does (WorkersCount = client count). Sender defaults to a single connection (ClientsCount=1).

If Command.Exec returns an error, or the codec fails, the server closes the whole connection and every in-flight Command on it fails; the author's stress test uses a FailCmd to drop connections this way. Send application errors back as Result values instead.

Cancelling or timing out ctx on the client only abandons the wait (Forget); the server keeps running the Command. SendWithDeadline sets a socket write deadline and does not pass a deadline to the server.

Core client bugs were fixed only recently: a deadlock on unexpected results (#4, May 2026) and keepalive breaking reconnect (#3, Apr 2026). Codec modules are pseudo-versioned, so pin a matched release set from VERSIONS.md.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over the Go siblings rpcx and Kitex (catalogued at 2.3-2.6x and 1.5-1.7x grpc-go, each on its own benchmark) when both ends are Go, you want the largest cut in per-request overhead, and you accept the command model. In its author's suite, cmd-stream/MUS reached 2.7-5.4x the QPS of Kitex run in gRPC-transport mode. Choose the gRPC-compatible siblings (grpcxx, wtx) or the C++ frameworks (brpc, SRPC) instead when you need cross-language clients or standard gRPC wire compatibility, which cmd-stream gives up.
verified_claims_summary: The run is the author's own go-client-server-benchmarks: localhost on one Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U laptop, Go 1.24.1, grpc-go v1.80.0 vs cmd-stream v0.7.1, 4 KB I/O buffers for every framework, a 30 ms server sleep per echo, and every request fired at once in its own goroutine. Over 1-16 connections, cmd-stream/MUS reached 145k-289k QPS against grpc-go's 46k-77k (3.1-4.6x); the Protobuf codec gave 2.4-3.5x and JSON 1.5-2.5x. A fixed burst of 100,000 requests finished 2.7-3.4x faster (0.38-0.61 s vs 1.03-2.09 s).
status_note: Maintained but quiet: the last commit on main is the v0.7.3 release (2026-05-07), and only dependabot PRs have arrived since. It is an MIT-licensed, go-gettable module, but pre-1.0 with frequent breaking releases and a single maintainer.
